verdicts.evidence: 'At the end of the story, why did Sun and Moon go up into the sky?' (because their house was overflowed with water and there was no room for them)
verdicts.rationale: The standard is an OR-list: any one student-performed purpose satisfies the clause. Students make use of the text "Why the Sun and the Moon Live in the Sky" to build knowledge and share information throughout the lesson. During Work Time A, students answer text-dependent questions (e.g., "At the end of the story, why did Sun and Moon go up into the sky?" — students respond "because their house was overflowed with water and there was no room for them"), turn and talk about setting details, and share out ideas. In Work Time B, students use puppets to role-play pages 7–17, further demonstrating knowledge built from the text. In Work Time C, students independently write what they know about the characters and setting. Multiple purposes (build knowledge, share information and ideas) are student-performed, satisfying the clause.

clauses.clause: Share individual writing with the group
Listen to others as they share their writing
Offer feedback on peers' writing
Respond to feedback received on own writing

verdicts.evidence: 'How can we work to become effective learners and care for the puppets?' (use them carefully so they do not break, put them away correctly, share nicely with each other, etc.)
verdicts.rationale: The resource partially meets 1.P.EICC.1.e. Students discuss the text with partners via turn-and-talk prompts (e.g., "At the end of the story, why did Sun and Moon go up into the sky?") and cold-call sharing, meeting the "discuss texts" clause. Students also touch on group norms when they discuss how to care for puppets ("use them carefully so they do not break, put them away correctly, share nicely with each other"), though this is reviewing/applying existing norms rather than fully developing new ones, so the norms clause is partially met. However, the lesson does not include any activity in which students share their own individual writing with the group, listen to peers share writing, offer feedback on peers' writing, or respond to feedback on their own writing — the writing activity (response sheets) is collected by the teacher with no sharing or feedback cycle. Four of six clauses are not met.

clauses.clause: Refer to parts of texts to support an idea, answer, or opinion (any one of idea/answer/opinion suffices — OR list)
clauses.note: Students refer to illustration details (parts of the text) to support their answer about the setting, but the reference is to visual details observed in the illustration rather than citing specific textual language/pages; other answers such as 'because their house was overflowed with water and there was no room for them' paraphrase story content but are not framed as explicitly referring back to a part of the text to support the answer. The act of referring to parts of texts is present but thin — students point to illustration details when prompted, yet the lesson never explicitly directs students to cite or point to specific words, sentences, or pages as textual support for their ideas/answers.

verdicts.evidence: 'As you look carefully at the illustration, what details help you understand the setting?' (huts or houses made of grass, a pathway, people in costumes, etc.)
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to refer to parts of texts when supporting an idea, answer, or opinion. Students do refer to illustration details to support their answer about the setting: "'As you look carefully at the illustration, what details help you understand the setting?' (huts or houses made of grass, a pathway, people in costumes, etc.)." This is a student-performed moment where students cite visual parts of the text to support an answer. However, the lesson does not explicitly direct students to refer back to specific words, sentences, or pages of the written text as evidence for their answers — the text-referencing is limited to illustration observation and content recall rather than deliberate citing of textual parts. Other questions (e.g., "why did Sun and Moon go up into the sky?") elicit recall-based answers without an explicit prompt to point to or cite a part of the text as support. The referring-to-text act is present but scoped narrowly to illustration details, making the clause partially met.
